newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch air cargo market shows life on some routes.
newsitem.headline: Dutch air cargo market shows life on some routes.

text.p: The ex-Amsterdam air cargo market has been set in its usual post-Christmas lull on many routes but some markets attracted unexpected business, a Reuters survey showed.

In anticipatioon of the slowdown, many individuals were taking annual winter sports holidays but some airlines and forwarders who remained at work said the first few weeks of January have not been as slow as they expected.

Rates, in keeping with the time of year, increased over Christmas but in January they are still holding firm in most of the markets apart from the Latin American and African sector. And currently there are no signs of any of the fuel surcharges being dropped.

Shippers have made their objections known about the surcharge and the matter has been taken to the Competition authorities in Brussels. In the Netherlands shippers are continuing to pay the fuel surcharge, said a spokesman of the Dutch shippers association.

Forwarders, on the other hand, are not keen on playing the middleman between the shippers and airlines in relation to the surcharge and on the whole think that the charge has involved a lot of extra administration, said several forwarders.
On the whole forwarders accept that something had to be done about the rates.
"It would have been fairer to introduce rates rises rather than surcharges to at least give them a chance to negotiate," said one forwarder.
But even with the surcharges, Schiphol's air cargo community has had a very busy Christmas. All types of air cargo players enthused about their hectic Christmas period.
Mischa de Boer, director of forwarder, MSAS, said: "There was simply no extra capacity, all the flights were fully booked."
However, despite the Christmas boom, airlines did not opt for more capacity. Airlines are showing that they are still cautious, said one source.

"Christmas was extremely busy in all of the markets. There was not enough capacity so shipments were refused or had to go by sea. Cargo was re-routed and there were considerable back-logs," said Peter Schoute, chairman of the Dutch air cargo carriers association, ACAN.
Though the back-logs have all been cleared, business is still good in January, he said.

Emery's Benelux manager, Koos Van Velzen, both the Netherlands and Belgium experienced significant growth in 1996. "Normally, Emery cancels some services over the Christmas and January period but this year we did not," he added. The company operates its own DC-8 freighter from Brussels.

Van Velzen puts the increase in business down to the demand for Emery's 24-hour products. "Companies are demanding more time sensitive services because they are carrying little or no stock." This is especially the case in the pharmaceutical, automotive and medical industries.

But this has led Emery to gain some new clients in the textile industry. "One-stop-shopping is another trend. Emery will be carrying out the sorting and distribution in Europe, with textiles that may have come in from the Far East or the U.S. The guaranteed lead times allow the companies to carry no stock," he noted.

The U.S. market particularly picked up towards the later part of 1996, with rates increasing dramatically and these have not shown any signs of dropping so far. Currently, rates to New York are 1.50 guilders per kilogram but they can go as high as 1.60 guilders per kilogram.

MSAS's De Boer said that the U.S. market was very busy and considering the time of year it still is. During Christmas MSAS had received several enquiries the day before companies wanted their shipments sent.
Giving one example De Boer said the company had one enquiry for the U.S. market concerning a 25 tonne shipment which had to go to the U.S. before Christmas.
Initially, the forwarder thought there was no possibility before early January because of the lack of capacity, however there was a cancellation. And these urgent requests were not unusual, he added.

North America generally is on an even keel after a busy Christmas, said Fred Veenendaal, director of VIA, GSA for Air Canada. The automotive industry and export of perishables out of the Netherlands provides stimulus for this market, he said. VIA had shipped one million kilograms of car engines to North America over the last few months, he added.
The Netherlands-Asian market has seen a few changes and currently it is extremely varied depending on the country, according to most Reuter sources.
Rates are holding firm currently, rates to Hong Kong are on average 2.80 guilders but these are expected to fall in the next few weeks.
Several Asian rates still retain a slight increase since before the Christmas rush.

Schiphol has seen China Southern Airlines begin its twice-weekly 767 service to Guangzhou and Beijing. Dutch cargo and charter carrier, Martinair, began its new Jakarta service and the Dutch carrier is set to begin its scheduled service to Guangzhou on January 23.

Administrative problems caused a delay in this service which was meant to start in October. Martinair has already operated some charter slights into the region but this will be the beginning of its weekly B747 scheduled service.
Taiwanese carrier, EVA is considering transfering two of its three freighter services to Brussels, while bringing in three passenger services into Schiphol but no firm decisions have been taken yet.

Gino Laan of Nippon Cargo Airlines said its freighters were full to Japan during the Christmas time. But the all-cargo carrier traditionally has a week's holiday in January and this year was no exception.
Narita airport gets very busy passenger-wise during the Christmas season and needs all of the slots, he said.
The Japanese airline's service started again on January 7.

Laan added that January is not as flat as expected, with bookings looking healthy. However, the carrier is hopeful a planned VAT increase in Japan expected for April/May time on imported consumer goods will provide a boost as companies try to import goods before the VAT is imposed.
De Boer of MSAS said a similar situation in China had led to a busy December, as China increased its import duties on January 1.
Korean Air operated a second freighter service in Novmber but this was stopped in January. A Korean Air source said the real problem was the cargo levels from Korea.
Industrial unrest in Korea concerning new labour laws is clearly hitting Korea's export business, he said.

The Middle East market is currently stable after a busy Christmas and New Year and rates are currently holding firm and they too have seen increased over the Christmas period. One forwarder said the market has been very active to the Middle East but it is now on an even keel.
Latin America has also had a very busy time over Christmas. The automotive industry is providing particular impetus for this region, said van Velzen.
Schoute said certain countries, such as Argentina and Brazil, offer a lot of potential for the development of the air cargo business, especially in the persihables and computer business.
Recently, Cargolux expanded its Latin America coverage when it added a third weekly frequency to Sao Paulo and it also began a new service to Santiago de Chile.

Rates in this market seem to have fallen slightly after the busy Christmas but extra capacity has gone into the market. Mexico City is around the 3.60 guilder level, while Santiago de Chile is 5.35 guilders per kilogram.
Africa is quiet at the moment. Frits de Bois of South African Airways said the first half of January has been flat because the South Africans are on their summer holidays.
Martinair's service to South Africa represents major competition for SAA in the Dutch market, sources said.
And several sources report that rates are under pressure.
Currently rates are still managing to hover around the 4.10 guilder level to Johannesburg but some forwarders said they have been offered rates as low as three guilders per kilo.

However, on a more optimistic note, there is a high demand for computer and electronic equipment in Southern Africa and many are expecting business to increase to Zimbabwe shortly as import licenses are expected to become easier to obtain.
